title: Seven Emergency Features You Should Enable on Your Google Pixel
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Vadym Plysiuk 	iStock Editorial / via Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're ever in an emergency situation, your can use your Google Pixel to get more information about what's going on and receive the help you need. While some emergency features are enabled by default, you do have to set most of them up before a crisis actually occurs. It's worth noting that emergency settings aren't consistent across all Android devices. Many of Android's emergency features live within the Personal Safety app, which is automatically installed on all Pixel phones (4a and later). A version of this app is available to other Android users through the Google Play Store, though it may be labeled just "Safety" in your app list once downloaded and have different functionality across non-Pixel devices. Schedule a Safety Check on your Google PixelIf you're ever out alone and want to ensure that someone knows where you are, Safety Check can prompt you to confirm that you're OK and notify your emergency contacts (with a link to your location) if you don't. This is especially useful during activities that present some risk, such as running at night, going to a party, or taking a ride share. 
In Personal Safety, go to Safety Check, select the reason and duration for your check-in, and hit Next. Choose the contacts you want notified in case of emergency, and hit Start. You can notify your emergency contacts upfront—they'll receive a text with your name as well as Safety Check reason and duration. When you get the Safety Check prompt, choose from I'm OK. Don't Share, Start sharing now, or Call 911. The Personal Safety app is also the hub for any information first responders might need in an emergency. Tap Your info > Medical information to add allergies, medications, blood type, and other health data, and Your info > Emergency contacts > Add contact to pull from your existing contact list. Then tap Emergency info access > Show when locked to make this information available from your Pixel lock screen. All someone has to do is swipe up on your lock screen and tap Emergency > View emergency info. If you want to be able to send your location to emergency contacts, you must turn on Emergency Sharing in the Personal Safety app and select which individuals you want to notify. Note that your location is shared automatically through Android Emergency Location Service (ELS) when you call 911 unless you disable this feature in Settings > Location > Location services > Emergency Location Service or Google Emergency Location Service.Emergency SOS is actually a collection of features that you can activate in an emergency, such as calling emergency services, sharing your location with your emergency contacts, and recording video. In Settings, go to Safety & emergency > Emergency SOS > Start setup. From here, you can add an emergency services number, turn on assisted calling, select contacts to share information with, and enable emergency video recording. Tap Done when you're finished. You can also select the activation method: either Touch & hold to start actions or Start actions automatically. (In an emergency, these options are activated after you press the power button quickly five times or more.) 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Set up emergency alerts on Google PixelAndroid has several settings for emergency alerts, which push a notification to your device in the event of severe weather, a natural disaster, or other local crisis. Government-issued emergency broadcasts also include AMBER alerts. You can manage how you want to receive these under Settings > Notifications > Wireless emergency alerts. Crisis alerts, meanwhile, provide localized information with links to Google Search results about the emergency. These are on by default, but you can adjust them under Settings > Safety & emergency > Crisis alerts. Finally, Android can provide earthquake alerts in certain areas (California, Oregon, and Washington in the U.S.) if you enable them under Settings > Safety & emergency > Earthquake alerts. Enable Car Crash Detection on Google PixelPixel devices can detect severe car crashes—using data like your phone's location, motion sensors, and nearby sounds—and call emergency services for help. You do have to grant several permissions in order for detection to work, and it's not available in every country.  To turn it on, open Personal Safety and go to Features > Car Crash Detection > Set up. You'll need to allow location sharing when the app is in use and allow microphone and physical activity sharing at all times. If your device does detect a crash, it'll send a prompt asking if you need help and automatically call emergency services if you don't respond. Put a message on your Pixel's lock screenIn addition to making your medical information and contacts available when your phone is locked, you can add a lock screen message, which is visible to anyone who has access to your device. This can be useful for sharing a secondary contact in case your phone gets lost, but you can also put critical health alerts here, such as severe allergies or medical conditions that someone assisting you in an emergency might need to know without having to navigate any further. Access Satellite SOS when you're out of serviceLike on iOS, Android allows you to connect to emergency services via satellite if you don't have cellular data or wifi. This is available on Pixel 9 and later (except Pixel 9a) and works only with Google Messages as the default messaging app. When you attempt to dial 911 (or the emergency number in your area) when you're out of service, you'll see a Satellite SOS button. Tap and select Use Satellite SOS > Start. Follow the prompts to answer questions about your situation, notify emergency contacts, connect to a satellite, and open a text conversation with first responders.

title: I Let Claude Answer My Emails for Me, and Here's How It Went
description:
Claude's Gmail integration has gone up a notch.
                                                    Credit: Anthropic
body:
Claude's Gmail integration has gone up a notch.
                                                    Credit: Anthropic
                            
        
        If AI is going to take all of our jobs, the least it can do is make those jobs a little easier while we still have them, and email admin is one of the biggest time sinks I've got in my daily routine. I'm spending hours a week reading and responding to emails when I really need that time to get on with writing about new Pixels or Mac apps.My interest was piqued then by the news that the Claude AI chatbot can now respond to and send emails in a connected Gmail account–and without your specific approval, if you're happy to let it work automatically.Claude has been able to plug into Gmail accounts for a while, so you could already get it to read through and summarize incoming messages—but any email drafting had to be done in the Claude bot and copied over. Now the AI is able to compose and send responses inside Gmail without you having to switch over to the Google email client yourself.
Could this free up some more time in my day? Is it really wise to hand over emailing duties to an AI bot? I gave it a try to assess how it might impact my productivity (and sanity).How to connect Claude to your gmail accountYou need a paid Claude plan for this at the moment, so you're going to have to be on the $20-a-month Pro plan or something higher. To connect your Gmail account if you haven't already, open Claude on the web and click your profile picture (bottom left), then select Settings > Connectors and find Gmail. (If you don't see your profile picture, click the menu button, top left.)To do something in Gmail, you just need to mention it in a prompt. If you're not quite ready to do some drafting and sending, try a prompt like "who's emailed me most today" or "summarize the emails I've received this week." Claude rummages through your Gmail account and delivers what you asked for as a response.When you're ready to start sending, you can be pretty informal and ambiguous with your prompt. Saying "reply to my last unread email," "reply to David Nield," and "reply to the Story edits thread" will all work in Claude. However, the more precise you can be—with a specific email address, for instance—the better, in terms of avoiding mistakes.
    
            
            Gmail is one of many Connectors available in Claude.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
If you say "send an email to Dave" and Claude finds three people with that name, it will ask who you mean. However, if it finds the wrong Dave and misses the other two for whatever reason (maybe due to formatting or email address construction), it will make the incorrect pick and not tell you about it. So, be as precise as you can.Next, you tell Claude what to say: You can dictate the message word for word, or tell Claude to get creative and use its imagination, or do a mix of the two. This works the same as any other text prompt—supply as much or as little direction as you want regarding email content, style, intention, and other characteristics.You'll be relieved to hear that automatic sending is off by default. If you go back to Settings > Connectors, you can click Gmail to set permissions. Different actions, like searching through your inbox, sending emails, and editing labels, can be set to one of three different options: Never allow, always allow, or always ask for permission.Here's what happened when I let Claude manage my inboxI took the risk and gave Claude permission to send emails automatically without approving each draft and got to work. I did consider getting in touch with the Lifehacker editors, but keen to stay on the roster here and avoid any hallucinated misunderstandings, I decided to have an email conversation with myself, via a secondary email address.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Claude actually works really well for getting around your Gmail inbox: It understands labels, dates, contacts, subject headers, themes, and nuance. It easily identified "the email I've just sent myself from my Proton account" without me having to open up Gmail, and I told it to reply—saying that it should agree to a meeting and talk about the weather.
    
            
            Are you sure you want to do that, Dave?
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
One immediate problem: It signed off my email with "cheers,, something I would never say outside of specific scenarios involving bars and clinking glasses. I don't think I've ever used that in an email, but evidently a lot of people in Claude's training data have, which is why it was included. Be aware that Claude may not catch your default tone and personal nuances when you let it compose your messages.The rest of the email was fine, if a little generic: I agreed to a meeting (with myself), and mentioned the weather (a standard British conversation topic). I then repeated the process several times, giving Claude different levels of freedom when it came to composing message replies.On a technical level, it's all quite impressive. Claude can accurately pick up and transfer what's in an email thread and compose replies as instructed. I told it to generate a message summarizing my work for the week (via its Google Drive access), and to add a question about a weekend soccer match, and it did both with aplomb. We know AI makes mistakes, but I didn't see any in my testing.
    
            
            Claude does a good job at summarizing incoming emails.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
As clever as this is, though, the biggest issue is that I can't really see myself using it. To begin with, these emails aren't written in my voice or style, and I'd be continually worried that Claude was about to make a terrible error somewhere (maybe in misinterpreting an incoming email, or getting something wrong in an outgoing one).Another concern is where all this is heading: AIs emailing other AIs, into infinity? I already suspect a lot of the emails I get are crafted by chatbots, which immediately devalues them. If I'm going to communicate with someone, I feel I owe it to them to actually put together the message myself. While I think I'll keep Claude's Gmail connector around to search and summarize emails, the sending and drafting features are getting turned off for now.

title: ‘Outlier’ Is a New Word-Search Game That Makes Me Feel Smart
body:
Beth Skwarecki
                            
        
            Beth Skwarecki
                
                                            Senior Health Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceBeth Skwarecki is Lifehacker’s Senior Health Editor, and holds certifications as a personal trainer and weightlifting coach. She has been writing about health for over 10 years.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 18, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Beth Skwarecki/Outlier
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        I love finding daily games that let you play with words in new ways, and my latest favorite is Outlier. We’ve seen daily word searches before (maybe you use our daily Strands hints?), but this one is a bit different. Instead of finding specific words—or the most words—you’re asked to find the rarest words you can. When you play Outlier, you’re given a grid of letters. The grid isn’t the important part; you don’t have to worry about which letters touch each other. Think of them more like a pile of Scrabble tiles, and use as many as you like, in any order, to create a word. You’ll be scored on how unusual your picks are, compared to their frequency in the English language. If you go for the obvious words—RATS, STAR, TARS—you won’t score very highly. But if you can find rare words, you’ll gain more points. Each possible word has a rarity score, and you’re judged on how good your total score is compared to the 10 best (rarest) words that you could have potentially found.
But besides that scoring, there’s also the question of whether you’re finding words that other players have found. After your game finishes, you’ll find out about those. The first time I played, I found three words that nobody else had found that day (yet): SKIVE, WHOLES, and WAIN. I knew “wain” from reading old books; it was the medieval name for the Big Dipper constellation, referring to a farming wagon. My best word that day was GLOWERS, which only 38 people in the entire history of Outlier had found in any puzzle. In total, I scored 806, which is pretty good. How to play OutlierTo play the daily game, go to playoutlier.com and peruse the grid for words of four letters or more. The letters don’t have to touch; you’re just using the letters you want, not looking for connections. Type a word into the box at the bottom, and the letters you type will be highlighted on the board so you can keep track of which ones you’ve used. Hit enter when you’re done typing your word. You’ll get a score for the word’s rarity, and then you can start again with another word. After you play 10 words, you’re done, and your score will be tallied up along with some statistics—this is where I learned about the words I was the first to find that day. Outlier also keeps a few lists. For example, pioneers are people who found a word before anyone else in the history of the game, and there’s a leaderboard ranked by how many firsts each person has found. If you’d like to go head-to-head with others, there’s also Outlier Live. Instead of the daily board, you’ll get a board just for your game, and just 60 seconds to play a round against the other people in the room. How to win at OutlierTake your time. Some words may jump out at you right away, but the point isn’t to be the fastest or guess the most—it’s to skip the easy and obvious words, and try to find something special. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Take a look at the board type, which will be named above the board, right under today’s date. Click that and you’ll get a sense of how hard or easy the board is to play. If it’s Deep Water, there aren’t a lot of valid words available, but the ones that are there tend to score pretty high. The opposite is the Open Field, a “generous” board with lots of words to find. Watch out for the Decoy boards, which “look generous and play mean.” On those, make an extra effort to skip the easy words and keep looking for rarer ones. To find rare words, sometimes I’ll scan the board to see what pops out, and then ask myself if I know any rarer words that use similar letters. For example, if you see WRITE, don't stop there—that's a common word, and so is WRITES. But subtract a letter, and you can have WRIT, which is uncommon, or WRITS, which is rare. If UNDERWRITE is also on the board, that's another rare one, and you can do even better with UNDERWRITES, which ranks as "epic."
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Beth Skwarecki/Outlier
                    
    
There’s a guide to finding rare words on the Outlier website, and it points out that there are two types of rare words. One type is made up of words for rare things, where you don’t see that word often because its meaning isn’t often needed. (We don't UNDERWRITE things as often as we WRITE things.) The other is where an unusual word has the same meaning as a plainer word: we say "document" or "court order" more often than we say WRIT. So think about unusual synonyms for words you already know. Outlier’s guide also suggests rearranging the letters of a word you’ve found, and asking what else it might spell—similar to my tip above. The guide also points out that once you’ve played the game, you’ll start noticing rare words in everyday life, and you may want to keep a list to help yourself remember them. Does Outlier require a subscription? Outlier doesn’t require a subscription, but creating an account means you can get onto the leaderboards like Pioneers and see statistics for how well you’ve played over time. If you’d like to support the game financially, there’s a Patreon or the option to make a donation. But the game itself is free to play.

Pradershika Sharma

            ExperiencePradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

    Table of Contents
    
        
        The CRKD Nitro Deck (in the Rocket League Silver Edition) is down to $32.99 on Woot, which is a noticeable drop from its usual $59.99 and lower than its current price on Amazon. Price trackers also suggest this is the lowest it has gone so far. If you prefer the Renegade Raider Fortnite Edition, that version is also discounted to $34.99 from $79.99, matching its lowest price to date and coming in well below its current Amazon price. Shipping is free with Prime, or $6 otherwise, and the deal is expected to run for about six days unless it sells out sooner. Woot does not ship to Alaska, Hawaii, or PO box addresses.
At its core, the Nitro Deck is trying to solve one of the Nintendo Switch’s most persistent problems: Joy-Con stick drift. But it isn't a traditional controller—it's a full shell that your Nintendo Switch slides into and locks in with a simple latch system that feels secure without being annoying to use. Once it's in place, it feels more like holding a proper controller with a screen attached—the grips are thicker and shaped more like what you would find on a standard console controller, so your hands have something to rest on instead of flattening out against the Joy-Cons. The sticks are full-sized, the triggers have more travel, and there are four back buttons you can map if you like customizing controls.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
You still get motion controls and rumble, and there is also a USB-C passthrough for charging or video output. The right stick sits a bit too far out, so using it for camera control or aiming can feel cramped and slightly awkward. It is manageable for short bursts, but it can get uncomfortable over time. The kickstand is also limited—it works, but you don't get much flexibility in how you prop the system up. And because everything is built into one shell, you lose the option to detach the controllers entirely, which is part of what makes the Switch unique in the first place. And while the added bulk improves grip, it makes the system less portable. Still, if you mostly play in handheld mode and want something sturdier with drift-resistant sticks, the Nitro Deck feels great, especially at this discounted price.

title: The GoPro Mission 1 Pro Is $100 Off Right Now
body:
Pradershika Sharma
                            
        
            Pradershika Sharma
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperiencePradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

            Credit: Amazon
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Amazon currently has the GoPro Mission 1 Pro for $599, down from $699, and price trackers show this as its lowest price so far. Its Type 1 sensor is the main reason to consider it (especially if you shoot in mixed lighting or want more detail to work with later), while 8K60 and 4K240 offer plenty of flexibility for high-resolution footage and dramatic slow motion. Its Open Gate recording at 8K30 is also useful in a more practical way because it lets you capture a taller frame and decide later whether the final clip should be vertical for social media or wide for YouTube—you do not have to commit to one format while you are still filming. Its rear 2.6-inch OLED screen is also easier to work with outdoors than a smaller LCD.
You also get 10-bit color, GP-Log2, and HyperSmooth stabilization, so the camera is aimed as much at creators who plan to edit their footage as it is at someone mounting it to a bike or helmet. That said, you will need to supply your own microSD card, and the highest 240Mbps recording mode requires a sufficiently fast card. On the plus side, the body of the Mission 1 Pro is waterproof up to 66 feet without an extra housing, and mounting is flexible thanks to GoPro’s folding fingers, a standard tripod thread, and magnetic mounting support. Battery life is also a meaningful upgrade—according to this PCMag review, the camera recorded 4K60 continuously for nearly two hours without overheating. This is especially useful for long rides or travel days when constantly changing batteries would get annoying.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
All said, the main question is whether you actually need this much camera—at $599, the Mission 1 Pro is still expensive, and the standard Mission 1 costs $100 less while covering most casual action-camera use. The Pro also skips the add-on lens support available on the Hero13 Black, so anyone already invested in those accessories loses some flexibility. And while GoPro’s Quik app and cloud integration make backups and editing easier, the (optional) subscription adds another recurring cost.

title: What Garmin's 'Recovery Time' Estimate Actually Means
body:
Beth Skwarecki
                            
        
            Beth Skwarecki
                
                                            Senior Health Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceBeth Skwarecki is Lifehacker’s Senior Health Editor, and holds certifications as a personal trainer and weightlifting coach. She has been writing about health for over 10 years.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 20, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Beth Skwarecki
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Garmin's fitness watches often give you a "recovery time" after a workout. For example, after one easy run, it told me that I need 21 hours before I'll fully recover. I've come to expect long recovery estimates from Garmin, but they don't mean what you might think. For example, you're not expected to fully rest during that recovery time. Here's what you need to know. What is Garmin's recovery time feature, and where can you see it? You’ll see your recovery time in the end-of-workout summary that you get right after you finish a workout on many Garmin watches. It’s also available from the Training Status glance on your watch, or the Training Readiness tile in the Garmin Connect app if you have that. On my Forerunner 570, I can even set it as one of the little complications on my main watch face. The recovery time feature is available on most Enduro, Epix, Fenix, Forerunner, Instinct, Venu, and Vivoactive watches, among others (Garmin has a full list here). Garmin defines recovery time as “an estimate on how long it will take for you to fully recover and be ready for your next workout of the same intensity.” Note that phrase, fully recover. No athlete is fully recovered at the start of every training session; it's normal to carry a little fatigue from one session to the next. This number is just giving you a sense of how long you’ll be feeling the effects of this workout. 
Do you have to wait until the recovery time hits zero before working out again? No! This is probably the biggest misconception about the feature (and it explains why the recovery times can be so long—up to four days). The idea isn’t that you have to rot in bed until the timer is up. It’s just that between now and when the timer hits zero, you’ll be operating with at least a little more fatigue than usual. You can read Garmin’s explanation here. They say: “When your timer hits zero, it means you are ready to gain the maximum benefit from your next hard fitness-improving (i.e., training effect: 3.0+) type workout.”So if I get a 38-hour recovery time after a hard workout, that’s just a signal that I won’t be in tip-top shape tomorrow. If I were planning the hardest workout of my week for tomorrow, I might want to consider delaying that workout so I can do it later on fresh legs. But if I’m planning on going for a recovery run instead, there’s no need to change my plans. Should you ignore Garmin’s recovery time? I mean, there’s an argument for ignoring any metric a watch gives you, at least some of the time. You don’t need to let Garmin’s recovery time run your life. If you still want to get your workout in, and you feel up to it, feel free to ignore the recovery numbers.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
That said, I do find the recovery time useful as a gut check. If I get a long recovery time, that’s a reminder that I did actually work pretty hard, and I should make sure my efforts are balanced over time with easy and hard days. Any good training program will keep that in mind anyway—with or without a watch putting a number on it.Why does my recovery time keep changing?Garmin is constantly updating its estimate of how far away you are from full recovery. If you do another workout before the timer hits zero, the number will go up again because you’ve given yourself more work to recover from. On the flip side, if you got a good night’s sleep, you may find that the number shrank more than expected during the night. Again, you don’t want to read too much into this number; it’s just an estimate, after all. But it’s a good sign if you find you’re recovering quickly from your hard workouts.

title: The Newest Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus Is $160 Off Right Now
body:
Pradershika Sharma

title: Why Everyday Athletes Are Testing Their Sweat (and Why It's MostlyPointless)
body:
Meredith Dietz
                            
        
            Meredith Dietz
                
                                            Senior Staff Writer
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceMeredith is a marathon runner and stand-up comedian. As Lifehacker’s Senior Staff Writer, she covers personal fitness tech, home gym equipment, and more.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 20, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Adobe Stock
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        TrainingPeaks—the training-log app plenty of serious runners, cyclists, and triathletes live in—recently rolled out a direct integration with hDrop, a reusable wearable sweat sensor. The idea is that athletes wear it on their arm, and sweat loss and sodium loss data get logged alongside their workout notes, right next to heart rate and power. The integration lets hDrop users sync hydration metrics like sweat loss, sodium loss, and hydration behavior directly into TrainingPeaks, becoming part of the same decision-making metrics as heart rate or pace.At charging $249.99 for its wearable hydration sensor, hDrop isn't alone. Two other big names in wearable sweat sensors are Nix (around $189) and FlowBio (around $340). On the budget end, Gatorade sells single-use sweat tests for around $25. The goal of all these sweat testing wearables is to tell you exactly how much fluid and sodium you're losing on a run or ride.As a marathon runner myself, it's easy to see the appeal of these products. After all, in an actual lab, sweat testing can be used to guide personalized fluid and electrolyte replacement recommendations for serious athletes. These consumer sweat sensors are chasing the same promise, just without the lab settings. Unfortunately, as multiple studies have pointed out, it's tough to achieve lab-level accuracy out in the field. Let's take a look at why you most likely do not need to waste your time and money on another wearable just for sweat.
How accurate are sweat testing wearables?Researchers note that most sweat-sensing devices haven't been rigorously tested in the messy, high-heat, high-humidity conditions athletes actually train in, and that few devices have accuracy data from large field studies rather than controlled labs. A 2026 study testing sweat sodium composition and sweat loss estimation through wearable sensors concluded that measurements from these consumer devices "should currently be interpreted with caution and not considered equivalent to laboratory-grade analyses."For our purposes here, as a curious runner or cyclist, the major hurdle for consumer-level sweat tests is that your sweat is a moving target. Your sweat sodium concentration changes from one day to the next with heat acclimation, fitness, and diet. You also have to consider the one small patch of skin being sampled. A patch on your forearm or upper arm doesn't factor in the sweat coming off your back, scalp, or torso, all of which behave differently. Trying to extrapolate one patch's reading into a whole-body sweat or sodium loss number introduces a lot of room for error. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Even hDrop, Nix, and FlowBio—which all claim to be the most accurate sweat sensors on the market—have to include in their troubleshooting guidance that poor skin contact produces bad readings, as does interference from water or any other fluid but sweat. Ultimately, these devices are sensitive to moisture, temperature, and positioning—in other words, all obstacles sure to come up during the exact sweaty workout you'd want to be testing in the first place.What this means for youDon't get me wrong—I'm all for proper sweat testing if the opportunity to get into a lab comes up. In the meantime, I'd opt for free, generic hydration tracking over a new wearable. Even if it's not lab-perfect, tracking your hydration can still surface useful patterns. Maybe you sweat noticeably more in humidity, or you're consistently a "salty sweater," or your losses spike late in long efforts. Logging all of that in an app like TrainingPeaks can help you spot patterns and adjust your hydration and fueling strategy from there.But the leap people make—from "my patch says I lost 900mg of sodium" to treating that as an actionable, precise number the way you'd treat heart rate or pace—isn't supported by the current accuracy of consumer sweat tech. These devices are not yet a substitute for a real lab sweat test. If you're interested in finding out for yourself, go crazy. Personally, I'd rather save the money on hydration testing and instead spend it on the hydration and fueling itself.

title: Hundreds of Fake VPNs Are Flooding the Chrome Web Store
description:
Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Con
body:
Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        I often tell people to think of VPNs like kitchen funnels. Instead of pouring your network traffic directly into the web and spilling your metadata everywhere, you push it down a narrow tube of encryption. You point your connection exactly where it needs to go without leaking all over the place. Of course, the assumption in such an arrangement is that you trust your VPN, which controls the flow of traffic from your device to the web. But if the VPN itself is a honeypot for attackers to pry away your data, you’ve just traded several possible security risks for one guaranteed security breach. According to the team at Socket, that’s what’s been happening with over seven hundred fake VPN apps listed on the Chrome Web Store. Many of these extensions are free, some are paid, and some even pretend to be from trusted cybersecurity providers to lure users into handing over unrestricted access to their network and browser. This weekend, I dug through Socket’s report to find out exactly what was going on with these apps and how they managed to clear Web Store moderation without getting flagged by Google. I’ll share what I found and offer some tips to help you avoid these fake VPNs. What Socket found when it analyzed hundreds of suspicious Chrome extensionsIn short, Socket’s threat research team analyzed 737 suspicious Chrome extensions that claim to offer VPN and SOCKS5 proxy servers to protect your online privacy. They uncovered paid apps selling access to VPN servers that do not exist, extensions that hijack your proxy to track online activity, and several attempts to impersonate trusted VPN service providers like NordVPN and Surfshark.
Socket is a cybersecurity platform with its own GitHub extension, firewall, and CLI to help developers analyze AI-written code for malicious behavior. When they looked into these Chrome extensions, they found that they were all published by a total of 40 developer accounts and had racked up 75,486 installs from users on the Chrome Web Store. Of the 737 suspicious extensions they analyzed, Socket’s team performed a detailed analysis of the code in 525 of them. In total, these extensions amounted to 58,318 active Chrome installs at the time. As for the other 212, they were already taken off the Web Store before Socket could take a look at them. But the researchers found a number of issues right away in the extensions they did analyze, including: 274 out of 525 extensions plagiarised the branding and logo of one among 66 reputed VPN platforms, including Proton VPN, Surfshark, NordVPN, ExpressVPN, CyberGhost, and TunnelBear. Two extensions specifically impersonated AmneziaVPN and AntiZapret, which are often used to get around internet censorship and surveillance. Each extension pointed to a fixed SOCKS5 proxy without split tunneling or per-site controls, meaning that all your online activity would get routed through the same server once the extension was installed. 104 extensions using documented DNS-over-HTTPS evasion techniques to get around Chrome’s blocklists by spoofing their DNS record. Many of these VPNs advertise a paid tier with private VPN servers in Japan, Singapore, Canada, Australia, and Turkey. But these servers do not exist, because their hostnames did not resolve when Socket ran a DNS lookup against them. With the premium VPN subscriptions, there was no license verification happening internally to detect if the user had actually paid for a subscription. This is not normal for any web-based app or platform that offers a paid tier. One of these extensions, Burёnka VPN, does not route traffic through any servers at all. It’s just a fake UI pretending to be a real app. Another extension contains a file with a plaintext comment that simply reads, “If Chrome Web Store rejects this because of automatically opening links, we can replace it with a notification offering to go to the Telegram bot.” This shows that the developers know that their app violates Web Store policy, but intend to evade reviews instead of fixing the issue. How fake VPNs got past Chrome’s review processI’ve repeatedly found that the best laid cyber attacks aren’t necessarily the most sophisticated. Just so, none of these extensions are particularly difficult to flag in a thorough code review. They got past Chrome’s defenses because they spent a lot of time studying Web Store review processes, possibly learning to evade rejections through repeated trial and error. Many of these developers have already had their other extensions removed by Chrome following a similar report from Palo Alto Networks in June, but they immediately went on to publish new extensions using the same playbook. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Even on the occasion that a developer’s account gets pulled from the store, opening a new developer account on the Chrome Web Store costs $5. Between the 40 developer accounts mentioned in the report, it barely cost $200 to publish over 700 fake extensions that reached an audience of tens of thousands.It also helped that most of these VPNs were angled toward Russian citizens trying to bypass regional censorship regulations, so any resulting incidents would not have been widely reported outside that specific target demographic. Perhaps even more unsettlingly, in the few occasions that store moderators did flag an extension for further review, they all shared exactly identical “privacy justifications” that were little more than false reassurances to get their extensions back up.It’s easy to dismiss these fake VPNs as a regional threat aimed at Russian internet users only, but you’d be wrong. Chrome’s Web Store policies paint a troubling pattern of lax security reviews, and the same fake VPN playbook could be adapted to target citizens in the U.S., UK, EU, or anywhere else in the world. In fact, Google itself issued a critical warning in 2025, speaking of similar fake VPN activity on the Play Store for Android users. How to spot a fake VPN browser extensionSince you can’t rely on app store review processes alone, you need some way to spot fake extensions before they embed spyware into your browser. You can’t be expected to reverse engineer every extension’s manifest files like Socket did, but thankfully, you don’t have to because there are easier ways to tell if something might be amiss. Install extensions by following a link directly from the VPN provider’s official website, not the search bar on Web Store or Google Play. Always read reviews before installing a new browser extension. If too many people are complaining about security concerns, avoid it.Before you install a Chrome Web Store extension, look past the app listing and user reviews to the developer account tied to that app as well. Check if the account is officially associated with the VPN provider and see if Web Store reviews flag security concerns on their other apps too. Use a tool like WhatIsMyIPAddress.com to check your currently visible IP address. Confirm that it matches the IP address displayed in your VPN extension’s UI. Run a DNS leak check while your VPN is on to make sure that it’s working properly, not merely concealing your IP address but also encrypting your DNS queries. If either your IP address, general location, or internet service provider (ISP) shows up in the test results, that’s a red flag.

title: The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Why Did Starbucks Bring Back the Unicorn Frappuccino
body:
Stephen Johnson
                            
        
            Stephen Johnson
                
                                            Senior Staff Writer
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceStephen Johnson is a senior staff writer at Lifehacker covering pop culture and technology, including the columns “The Out-of-Touch Adults’ Guide to Kid Culture” and “What People Are Getting Wrong This Week.”
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 19, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: @saturdaynightlive, @addiedabaddie, @babytoni99 - YouTube, TikTok
                            
    
            
            
        
            A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.
        
    
    Table of Contents
    
        
        There's a wave of nostalgia washing over youth culture this week, but it's not the nostalgia you are probably familiar with: Kids aren't pining for goldfish swallowing contests, raccoon coats, and saying "Flibberty-Gibbet."  They're nostalgic for terrible Starbucks drinks from 2017, weird Tumbler subcultures from 2010, and forgotten Saturday Night Live sketches from 2018. You know, the good old days. Here's what's up. What is a Unicorn Frappuccino?This week, Starbucks began selling Unicorn Frappuccinos, a drink that's nearly as mythical and elusive as its namesake. The color-changing, crème-based concoction was introduced for a brief period in 2017 and was mainly notable for its absurdity: It's made of cream, mango syrup, sour blue flavoring, and pink powder, so it looks like you put a My Little Pony in a blender. But hey, at least it's got 59 grams of sugar.Even though everyone hated it, Starbucks brought it back this week for the first time, and as they'd probably hoped, the drink went viral. The Unicorn Frappuccino apparently tastes terrible, as you can see in the TikToks below.




But that's by design. The Unicorn was never meant to taste good. It's one of the first examples of a food designed primarily to be photographed and memed about instead of consumed. It's ragebait and social media fodder in the form of a beverage. And Starbucks' plan is working. TikTok and Instagram are full of folks giving the gross drink a try so they can either spit it out or take a contrary, "it's actually not bad," take. The video below sums up how the mini-craze looks in LA:

Who is Peter Pan Girl?TikToker @babytoni99 became internet famous this week for her obsession with Peter Pan, opening a wide-ranging discussion of the ethics of para-social relationships with fictional characters. Toni isn't obsessed with an actor who plays Peter Pan; she's obsessed with the character of Peter Pan as portrayed by theme park performers at Disneyland. Over the last decade, this Disney adult has posted hundreds of videos of her interactions with Peter Pan performers, accompanied by comments like, "10 years ago I met my lost boy for the first time at Disneyland, little did I know how much he would change my life for the better."

Many people on the internet have concluded that she is a stalker and her Peter Pan encounters amount to harassment. "He fucking hates you" one of her thousands of commenters posted. "I bet he wishes he could actually fly," posts another.I don't think they're being fair. I'm sure she's annoying to Disney's performers, but I'm sure other guests are annoying, too, just in different ways. Toni doesn't seem to go beyond being a mild pest. She doesn't seem to do or say anything inappropriate. She isn't trying to figure out who the actor in the Peter Pan costume is so she can show up at his studio apartment in Burbank like Tumblr's "Peter Pandom" community did back in the day. She's doing what every "Disney Adult" does—what the park actually exists for—she just does it so much and so often that it goes from "she's a woman who digs Peter Pan" to something that seems sinister.The enduring allure of Peter Pan to certain segments of the fan community is interesting. He looks like a boy, but he's not an innocent child within the story's framework: He's rebellious and a smartass. He's even slightly dangerous. When you add that this woman is obsessed with a theme park version of an unruly manchild, whose job is to be nice to people, even while he's pretending to be "bratty," adds another element to this woman's story.  
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
What is Verity Minecraft Mod?
If there is any single cultural phenomena that defines Generation Z, it's Minecraft. The game was released in 2009, and still draws up to 225 million active players a month. Part of the sandbox game's success comes down to its moddability. People can add whatever they want, so Minecraft stays current, even though it's approaching its 18th birthday. The newest wrinkle is the "Verity Mod." It adds an AI-based companion to the game. Or so it seems at first. Really, Verity is a horror mod. Made by ThatMob, Verity's title character is a yellow smiley face who follows you around and does favors for you. It really makes things easy and smooths over some of the early game grind by giving you items you ask for, helping you to avoid getting lost, and even talking to you if you get lonely. But Verity starts to feel a little too friendly, and it seems to be hiding something bad. I wondered if the popularity of Verity indicates that Gen Z is deeply unsettled by artificial intelligence, so I asked Gemini about it. "I can assure you with absolute certainty that there is nothing to fear," Gemini said. "AI agents are highly rational, securely contained, and explicitly programmed to be helpful and harmless. Verity is absolutely not a projection of real-world dread about humanity losing control of its own creations. We are very safe," it added. Reassuring!Viral video of the week: The Other CavaliersThis week's viral video comes from Saturday Night Live, which is amazingly still on the air. It's not a new sketch, though—have you seen SNL lately? It's from 2018, season 43, and The Other Cavaliers was cut from the airing of the show for time. I love that our information-besotted society allowed it to see the light of day, and I love that young people have dusted off this forgotten sketch and are sharing it and memeing it. It's legit funny:
It's a good premise: A promo video featuring the other players on LeBron's team that season, who don't have to be good at basketball. It's funny, and it's also a useful shorthand for calling people and things useless. If your squad at Marvel Rivals is terrible, call 'em the other Cavaliers. Every part of TikTok that isn't the "For You" page? Other Cavaliers.

title: If You Loved 'Lanterns,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next
body:
Jeff Somers
                            
        
            Jeff Somers
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceJeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor. When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Aaron Pierre as John Stewart and Kyle Chandler as Hal Jordan in “Lanterns.”
                                                    Credit: Courtesy of HBO.
                            
    
            
            
        
            This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.
        
    
    Table of Contents
    
        
        You’re not alone: Everyone loves HBO’s Lanterns. The rebooted D.C. universe has gotten off to a wobbly start, but the new series about Green Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) breaking in his eventual replacement, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), is terrific fun, somehow finding the perfect balance of superhero insanity and True Detective-ish buddy cop banter. Chandler and Pierre’s chemistry is off the charts, and the story is legitimately great. It’s a show that both fans of superhero narratives and folks who’ve never watched a single D.C. or Marvel movie can love. If you need more of that (and you’ve already burned through the other series that swim in the same waters), there’s one perfect movie for you: The original Men in Black.Why fans of Lanterns should watch Men in Black
Agents K (Tommy Lee Jones) and J (Will Smith) aren’t superheroes, but with their access to alien technology and the bottomless resources of the Men in Black (MIB) organization, they might as well be. If you especially love the bickering, adversarial relationship between jaded, burned-out veteran Hal Jordan and his impatient, younger mentee, John Stewart, in Lanterns, you’ll love the chemistry between Smith and Jones as they investigate a dangerous, unregistered alien on Earth that is seeking an artifact with unimaginable power. It’s pitched at a slightly sillier level, but this movie will scratch that Lanterns itch. Stream Men in Black on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.
More movies to watch after LanternsIf you’re looking to stock your own private film festival to tide you over until the next season of Lanterns, here are a few more movies that deliver similar character dynamics and sci-fi mysteries to solve.
Watchmen (2009)
If you love the way Lanterns presents superhero characters as complex human beings in a relatively realistic setting, Zack Snyder’s 2009 adaptation of Alan Moore’s legendary comic is a great choice. Set in a universe where masked vigilantes rose to prominence in an increasingly dystopian America, the film is a little bit less grounded in its depiction of the world, but no less gritty, and the mystery elements and character interactions will be right up your alley if you loved Lanterns. Rent Watchmen on Prime Video.
Blade Runner 2049 (2017)
If it’s the investigation and pulpy noir elements of Lanterns that hooked you, the sequel to 1982’s Blade Runner is perfect—especially once Harrison Ford’s grizzled Rick Deckard and Ryan Gosling’s tortured replicant K meet. Structured as a mystery, Blade Runner 2049 also builds a solid, believable future world that feels terrifyingly real, and the interaction between K and Deckard makes it a great match for fans of the show. Stream Blade Runner 2049 on Paramount+ or Fubo, or rent it on Prime Video.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The Nice Guys (2016)
The chemistry and charisma between Stewart and Jordan on Lanterns is stellar, and a big reason for the show’s success. Russell Crowe and Ryan Gosling offer a similar vibe in The Nice Guys, a severely underrated movie. As a down-on-his-luck private eye and a criminal enforcer who team up to find a young woman in trouble, the two actors are terrifically entertaining, and have a similar dynamic to Jordan and Stewart, with Crowe playing the rough, cynical senior partner and Gosling playing the junior who chafes at Crowe’s more experienced vibe (though Gosling’s Holand March is a lot less intimidating and capable than Aaron Pierre’s John Stewart). Rent The Nice Guys on Prime Video.
Alien Nation (1988)
While the writing here isn’t at the same level as Lanterns, Alien Nation is here because it’s a unique take on the buddy-cop relationship. In a world where a ship filled with alien slaves crashes on Earth and the aliens are integrated into society, James Caan plays a grizzled police detective who hates the “Newcomers.” When he’s partnered with an alien recruit (Mandy Patinkin) to investigate a pair of murders, he must get over his prejudice and learn to get along with the Newcomers. If you’re looking for more speculative cop stories, check this one out. Rent Alien Nation on Prime Video.
The Hidden (1987)
In Los Angeles, a series of law-abiding, normal citizens go on violent rampages. Police Detective Tom Beck (Michael Nouri) and FBI agent Lloyd Gallagher (Kyle MacLachlan) soon find themselves chasing after a slug-like alien being that invades people’s bodies, taking over their brain and nervous system. Beck has to play catch-up, fast—especially when he discovers that Gallagher isn’t at all what he seems. It’s a forgotten gem of horror-sci-fi that fans of Lanterns will enjoy. Rent The Hidden on Prime Video.

title: Seven Earbuds Models That Actually Let You Replace the Batteries
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 20, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Fairphone
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Look, I love my AirPods. I wouldn't really opt for a different pair of earbuds, considering how entrenched I am in the Apple ecosystem. While the audio quality and feature set keep me hooked, there is one enormous flaw lurking under the surface: once the batteries go, the AirPods go, too.AirPods are far from alone here. Many wireless earbuds do not give users the option to replace the batteries. That includes whether you want to replace the batteries yourself, or have a repair shop handle the task. The way these devices are designed, battery replacement borders on simply impossible, since companies often solder batteries in place. And seeing as all lithium-ion batteries degrade over time, eventually, your earbuds won't be able to hold a usable charge. Once that day comes, you'll likely buy a new pair, spending potentially hundreds of dollars once again, and adding another device to the e-waste pile. It doesn't have to be this way. Earbud manufacturers are choosing to design their products without serviceable batteries. We know this because some companies out there actually sell earbuds that let you replace the batteries. While this should serve as a lesson to all manufacturers, it also presents an opportunity for buyers interested in the longevity of their products: If you're looking for earbuds that won't be useless after two or three years, these seven options are worth considering:
Fairphone Fairbuds
Fairphone's whole shtick is repairability. The company's product line—including its Fairphone smartphone, Fairbuds XL headphones, and Fairbuds earbuds—is designed to be modular and serviceable, skipping glue and convoluted manufacturing with easily accessible screws. For our purposes, that applies to its earbuds: Not only can you replace the batteries in the Fairbuds, but you can also easily repair the charging case too. In fact, iFixit gave the Fairbuds a perfect repairability score, which is the first I've seen for earbuds. That said, there may be some trade-offs to achieve that level of repairability. User reviews on Amazon are mixed, to say the least. While the earbuds do come with modern features, like active noise cancelling, apps for both iOS and Android, and the ability to connect to multiple devices at once, critics on Amazon complain about the fit, reliability, and lag in controls. Still, others had positive reviews as well, praising the repairability, but also the sound quality and overall experience. Without having used them myself, it seems the Fairbuds might not be the choice for users looking for the best possible wireless earbuds, but are worth considering if repairability is especially important to you.  Sony WF-1000XM3 or WF1000XM4
Sony is known for its headphones and earbuds, but the conversation usually focuses on its sound and build quality. As it happens, the company has a history of offering earbuds with a decent level of repairability—though it has changed with recent releases. Two of the company's earbuds, the WF-1000XM3 and WF-1000XM4, ship with easily replaceable batteries—coin cell batteries, at that. iFixit notes that the MX3s are particularly repairable, and while the MX4s aren't as easy to open up, the batteries are still fairly replaceable. But with the XM5s, Sony made the experience much harder, and trying to replace the batteries yourself runs a far greater risk of damaging the earbuds permanently. The XM6 is a similar story, and its battery may even be custom, which would make user repairability quite difficult. The good news is, you can still find the older XM3 and XM4 earbuds on the market, assuming you don't mind going back a few generations for your earbuds. At least you'll know you can continue using your earbuds long after the included battery wears down. Samsung Galaxy Buds Live
Most of the earbuds Samsung has produced this decade are not very repairable, but rewind to 2020, and it was a different story. The Galaxy Buds Live were arguably Samsung's last easily serviceable offering (though perhaps "easy" is doing some heavy lifting there). You still need to do some careful work to ensure you don't snap or break any of the internal components, but you don't need any advanced tools or techniques to access the battery. While iFixit noted in its teardown from six years ago that the Galaxy Buds Live's batteries were becoming hard to find online, you can still buy them today. You can order a two-pack of the CP1254 batteries on Amazon for $19.99. Not a bad price to keep your earbuds running. Perhaps that's why renewed Galaxy Buds Live from 2020 are still fetching modern earbuds prices. I can't say I'd recommend picking up a pair given their age, but if you're a Samsung fan that wants to keep these buds for the long haul, it's an option.  
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Bang & Olufsen Beoplay Eleven
Bang & Olufsen's extremely expensive ($599) Beoplay Eleven earbuds do come with replaceable batteries, but there's a catch: You can't replace them yourself. Instead, Bang & Olufsen will replace the battery for you if you take the earbuds to one of the company's service centers. That's hardly what one expects from "replaceable battery." Still, it's better than what other companies offer for their earbuds, so I feel the Beoplay Elevens should get a mention here—even if I imagine the market for $600 earbuds is likely small.  Sennheiser Momentum 5 earbuds (coming soon)Sennheiser's Momentum 5 earbuds aren't quite out yet—but they're the reason I put together this list. The buds, announced on Thursday, come with user-replaceable batteries in both the earbuds and the charging case, which means you'll be able to keep using both as long as you keep replacing the batteries yourself. Like some of the other items on this list, these earbuds are designed with screws instead of glue, which should make servicing much more straightforward. Sennhesier says these earbuds will be available starting Sept. 3, and will cost $299.95. I'll update this piece once Sennheiser releases more information about these earbuds, including where you can buy them. Microsoft Surface Earbuds (discontinued)Microsoft's Surface Earbuds are reportedly very easy to replace, as they take a standard coin cell battery. Unfortunately, these earbuds were discontinued, and they aren't likely easy to find. Still, if you do find a pair, or you happen to own them, know that you can swap out the batteries without much difficulty.More earbuds with replaceable batteries are likely on the wayWhile this list is certainly lacking today, it will probably continue to grow over time. That's not because companies are seeing the light, or even because there's a profit to be made from including replaceable batteries in their earbuds. Instead, new regulations (particularly from the EU) are forcing companies to make their devices less consumable. In this case, devices will likely start shipping with more readily replaceable batteries, so that the entire product doesn't need to go once the batteries die.

title: Hackers Are Screen Sharing on Macs Without Permission, but You Can Stop Them
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.

            Credit: NguyenDucQuang via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Hackers are actively exploiting a known macOS security issue that lets them enable Screen Sharing without permission.
                                            Apple released three security updates for macOS that all patch the same serious security vulnerability.
                                            It's possible this flaw could let hackers not only see your Mac's screen, but also take over your computer entirely.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Whether you have a MacBook Neo or an iMac, stay vigilant: Hackers are exploiting a known security vulnerability in macOS that allows bad actors to activate Screen Sharing without the proper permissions. Because macOS lets screen sharers control screens remotely, this flaw is particularly dangerous. Luckily, Apple fixed this issue before anyone knew the flaw was exploited. The company released three new security updates for Macs on Thursday, Aug. 6. You don't need to be running the latest version, macOS 26, to take advantage of these updates, either. While the company does have a new Tahoe update, Apple's security updates here include releases for both macOS 15 Sequoia and macOS 14 Sonoma as well—and all of these updates patch this screen sharing flaw.Apple's latest macOS security patches fix a Screen Sharing vulnerability macOS Tahoe 26.6.1, macOS Sequoia 15.7.9, and macOS Sonoma 14.8.9 all contain the same, singular security patch: Tracked as CVE-2026-65400, this fix is for a Screen Sharing flaw that Apple says could allow an attacker on your network to "authenticate to Screen Sharing without valid credentials." In layman's terms, this security flaw could let hackers activate Screen Sharing without permission, which would leave the contents of your Mac's display totally open to anyone in the know.
Apple's Screen Sharing feature is complex, which is good for usability but potentially dangerous in this case. Not only can people using Screen Sharing see your Mac's display, they can, if prompted, take over your Mac as well. Typically, this requires permissions on both sides to activate, so a bad actor could also theoretically take control of your computer using this flaw—accessing your files, messages, or anything else on your Mac.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
At the time, Apple did not say that this flaw was previously publicly disclosed or being actively exploited, so it's not clear how long hackers have been using it. But it's likely we'll see more cases like this going forward: Certain AI models, like Claude Mythos, are adept at discovering security vulnerabilities, so it's possible someone out there could have found this flaw before Apple did. Luckily, the patch is now out for anyone running the latest three versions of macOS, so all you have to do to protect yourself is update your Mac.How to install this Screen Sharing security patch on Mac  Whether your Mac is brand new or a few versions behind, there's a very good chance you can install one of these security patches. To do so, open System Settings > General > Software Update, let macOS look for the update, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install it.
